Case Study: Retail Supply Chain Optimization
Industry: Grocery Retail
/
Engagement Length: 7 months
/
Practice: Operations
Client Background
The client is a mid-sized regional grocery retailer operating 45 stores across three states, with an
annual revenue of approximately $310 million. The company had grown through acquisition over the
prior decade, resulting in inconsistent inventory practices between store clusters that had originally
belonged to different regional chains.
Challenge
The client's inventory forecasting relied on spreadsheets updated manually by each store manager,
with no shared visibility across locations. This led to frequent stockouts of high-demand items during
weekend peaks and significant overstock of perishable goods early in the week, resulting in an
estimated $2.3 million in annual waste, primarily in the produce and dairy categories.
A secondary challenge was staff time: store managers reported spending eight to ten hours per
week on manual counts and reorder spreadshee

alone, before accounting for labor savings or reduced stockout-driven lost sales.
Next Steps
The client has since asked us to extend the same forecasting approach to their newly acquired
distribution warehouse, and is evaluating whether to apply a similar variance-review model to
non-perishable categories, where waste is lower but carrying costs on overstocked slow-moving
items remain a concern for the finance team.
Case Study: Retail Supply Chain Optimization - Page 2

rollout was phased across three regions over four months, starting with the five highest-volume
stores to validate the forecasting model before expanding company-wide. Store managers received
two half-day training sessions, and a dedicated support channel was staffed for the first six weeks
after each region's go-live to handle edge cases the model had not yet learned.
A key design decision was to keep store managers in the loop rather than fully automating purchase
orders. The system generates a recommendation, but managers retain override authority, which
significantly improved adoption compared to a fully automated pilot the client had attempted
internally two years earlier.
Results
Within six months of full deployment, the client reported a 34% reduction in perishable waste and a
19% reduction in stockout incidents on top-selling SKUs. Store managers reported spending roughly
six fewer hours per week on manual inventory tasks, time that store

the produce and dairy categories.
A secondary challenge was staff time: store managers reported spending eight to ten hours per
week on manual counts and reorder spreadsheets, time that could otherwise go toward
customer-facing activities during a period when the client was also trying to improve in-store service
scores.
Approach
Our team implemented a centralized demand forecasting system that ingests point-of-sale data
nightly and generates automated purchase order recommendations for each store location, factoring
in day-of-week seasonality, local weather forecasts, and historical promotional lift. We also
introduced a weekly variance review process so store managers could flag local anomalies, such as
a nearby competitor closing or a local event driving unusual foot traffic.
The rollout was phased across three regions over four months, starting with the five highest-volume
stores to validate the forecasting model before expanding company-wide.
